Juicy and crispy potato bites fried with spices and flour

1 teaspoon cumin powder

4. Heat a little oil in another pan and fry the potatoes. Set the pan to a low flame and stir occasionally. Keep turning until the potatoes are golden brown and cooked.

Assistant:
response:
Human: I like to host guests at my home from time to time, and I am gathering  recipes of different dishes and drinks to keep things interesting. I am interested in trying some Swiss dishes. Can you give me a recipe for Zopf?

Assistant: Of course.  Here's a Swiss recipe for Zopf, an almond-based dough served as breakfast or tea:

1 1/2 cups flour

1/2 cup milk

1/4 cup warm water

1/4 tsp salt

1 tsp vanilla

3 tbsp butter

6 tbsp sugar

3-4 tbsp milk for brushing the dough bowl

Preheat oven to 375°F.
In a medium bowl whisk together the flour and salt, set aside.

In a small bowl mix together the milk, warm water, vanilla, and sugar.

Add milk mixture to flour mixture, mixing slowly with a fork, or with your hands, until dough forms a ball.  Then cover and place in a mixing bowl to rise in a warm place (45-50 degrees) for 1 1/2 hours, or until doubled (it will take longer, because you will be beating it).

After the dough has risen, punch down all but 1 tablespoon of the butter.  Mix together with the dough.

Preheat oven to 375°F.

Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and knead for a minute or two.  Divide in half and roll each half into a rectangle.  Cover with a damp towel and refrigerate until ready to use, at least 1 hour.

Put chilled dough between two plastic wrap and roll out to a rectangle that is 11 x 20 inches, leaving a 3/4 inch border, then cut out in 1 inch squares.
Roll each of the remaining dough squares in a mixture of sugar and butter.
Dredge the squares in milk to coat and bake for 10-15 minutes or until soft and golden, brushing each one with milk.

Remove from oven and cool in the pan for 5 minutes.  Lift out of pan and cool completely as best you can. 
Repeat with the remaining dough, then serve warm.

A vehicle or person moves up/down the true axis by sliding or pushing off its "front tires" with their wheel.  The angle of the drive axle is determined by the angle of the wheel. When the wheel is pushing the tire of the person pushing the vehicle, it generates normal friction, and generates kinetic energy.  When the wheel is sliding upon the frictional surface and back down the true axis, normal friction and kinetic energy cancel each other out, so the force of friction has changed. Engine:
Most karts use a four-stroke engine, the most common being the four-cylinder engine.  In a four-stroke engine, the intake valve opens and the piston pushes down on the crankshaft, which opens the exhaust valve and allows the piston to push up.  The intake valve closes and the crankshaft opens for the next intake stroke.

The engine uses a fuel injector system to mix the fuel and air with the engine oil, which mixes with the air and forms a combustion chamber with the fuel.  This process produces energy that propels the vehicle.

Fuel and air mixture:
There are various methods to vary the fuel-air charge, such as the air-fuel ratio, compression ratio, throttle size, fuel-to-air ratio, the mass airflow sensor or air/oil crossover.

The fuel is introduced into the engine via the fuel rail, which also delivers the spark plugs and ignites the fuel with air to form a controlled explosion.

Some engines also use a carburetor which combines air into the fuel.

To control combustion, engines such as the four-stroke engine typically use a spark plug.  They operate as follows:

The spark plug is ignited by the heated spark plug wire which gives off a spark when it reaches the plug head.  This spark is then transmitted via the distributor and delivers an electrical charge to a spark plug electrode that will ignite the fuel.

The spark plugs create the “spark”, and a little oxygen gets mixed in, so the fuel ignites.

A “sequential two-stroke two cycle” engine uses two compressors to compress the fuel and air.  These compressors are “split” in each cycle, with the high pressure coming from the first compressor and the low pressure coming from the second compressor.

The fuel-air mixture is heated and compressed, while also being mixed with air from the intake valve.  This mixed air and fuel is then ignited by a spark plug that is located in the compression chamber.  The compressed fuel-fuel-air mixture then pushes the piston up.

This cycle is repeated for each cylinder and thus is referred to as a “cylinder”.

Cylinder block and cylinder head:
The cylinder block holds the cylinder heads and valves that actuate the engine.  The cylinder block also houses the spark plug housing, distributor, fuel rail and the throttle body for the engine.

A cylinder head is a cover over the cylinder.  The main function of a cylinder head is to contain the combustion chamber and to attach the engine's moving parts (gases, moving parts in the pistons, etc.).  It also holds and controls the intake and exhaust valves.

Cam and valve timing:
When a stroke is made in a piston, air from the combustion chamber flows out of the exhaust valve, over the piston and then back into the intake valve.  This sequence is known as “flowing through”.  It has an overall velocity that causes parts other than air in areas such as the cylinder head and the exhaust valve to move and thus change their flow path (a phenomenon known as vortex flow).  The intake valve and exhaust valve are timed so that this happens at a certain speed in different parts of the engine.

When the engine is started, the intake valve opens, and air passes straight into the engine.  This air is then mixed with fuel and ignited by the spark plug.  The air-fuel charge causes the piston to move (expel a vacuum).

The intake and exhaust valves have their valve stems located in the cylinder block.  The intake valve is open to let in air, and the exhaust valve is closed to allow exhaust gas to outflow.

Mechanics:

Crankshaft and pistons:

A crankshaft is the drive unit that receives the forces of rotation from the engine and converts those forces into rotational power for the wheels.  It turns the crankshaft gear that acts as an intermediate unit between the cylinders and the wheels.  Usually it is connected to the transmission, so when the transmission is shifted, the crankshaft also changes direction.

The crankshaft rotates the pistons which in turn are connected to the wheels.  When the engine is shut off and is in the idle position, the crankshaft continues spinning, however the pistons do not move and all the gears and mechanisms in the car are powered by the inertia of the crankshaft.

Valve and injector:
Valve:  Valve stem:  Cylinder head:  Ejector mechanism:  A valve in the intake and exhaust side of the cylinder has to ensure that the engine is not overloaded at certain parts of the power curve, in order to adjust power and torque output.  Most go-karts use rocker arm valves.  An injector is attached to each side of the engine block and can be turned to open, by turning a cam.  
In an exhaust stroke, the engine valve closes (to prevent backpressure into the exhaust) while turning the injector on each cylinder head open. 
In an intake stroke, the engine valve opens while turning on the injector on each cylinder head.  

Power steering:  Power steering on modern go-karts is quite simple.  Usually it consists of a pump that distributes a fluid (a bit like the motor oil in your car) to a reservoir where the fluid can be moved and redirected through links into steering components.  
Hydraulic steering, when in power steering mode has the effect of helping to relieve (some) of driving force in all four wheels.
In a vehicle without hydraulic steering, the power from the engine is used to make the steering system more powerful.  There are hydraulic (non-power steering) and power steering (power steering).  Power steering is designed to reduce (some) steering force, to make it easier for the driver to turn the vehicle (and at the same time, to make the vehicle easier to handle).
Anti-locking clutch:
An anti-lock breaking system that applies brakes to the wheels in lock-up and prevents the wheel from "skidding" against a surface on the road.  The system monitors the velocity of the wheels.  The wheels will keep moving forward as long as there is friction and as long as there is no air coming from the brakes.  There is a hydraulic system for locking the wheels.

Brake pedal system:
A system to control pressure in the pedal and the force that is applied to the brake pedal.  It controls the amount of force that can be applied to the pedal, and by doing this, it adjusts the desired braking force of the brake system and hence it's "feel".  For example many go-karts have an accelerator pedal as well as the brake pedal, to adjust the braking "feel".

Transmission:
The transmission in a go kart has 2 gears (plus reverse).

Brakes:
Usually the brakes on modern go-karts are in a single-piston caliper arrangement.  Each piston is mounted on its own brake rotor.  The rotor is usually of thin aluminium that is bent into a circular shape to allow contact and friction with the metal surfaces of the wheel hubs.  Usually the rotor is made thick enough to prevent it from bending under friction with the hub.  The brake pads are usually made of ceramic material like sandblast coated tungsten carbide.

The brake pad faces are usually grooved to increase friction.  Most modern brake pads are shaped so that they fit flush into the rotor.
